claims.text: The baseline material is an as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
The baseline HfMoTaTiZr density is approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
The baseline HfMoTaTiZr room-temperature yield strength is approximately 1600 MPa.
The baseline HfMoTaTiZr yield strength at 1000 °C is approximately 855 MPa.
Replacing a controlled portion of Hf with Al will reduce alloy density.
Adjusting or increasing Nb will offset potential losses of ductility caused by Al substitution.
The Al- and Nb-modified alloy will retain the baseline room-temperature yield strength.
The Al- and Nb-modified alloy will retain the baseline elevated-temperature yield strength.
The modified alloy will remain a BCC solid solution.
Al substitution will make the lattice less dense because Al is a low-density element relative to the refractory constituents.
The modified BCC phase will maintain solid-solution strengthening.
Balanced Nb and Mo/Ta contributions will preserve favorable dislocation mobility.
Mo contributes to higher room-temperature strength in this Hf-containing refractory-alloy family.
Mo, Nb, and Ta contribute to elevated-temperature strength.
The modified alloy will have approximately 10% lower density than the as-cast baseline.
The modified alloy's room-temperature yield strength will remain within approximately 10% of 1600 MPa.
The modified alloy's 1000 °C yield strength will remain within approximately 10% of 855 MPa.
Performance will be evaluated by quasi-static compression at room temperature and 1000 °C.
The substitution limit is uncertain because Al may alter dislocation behavior, phase stability, or fracture toughness.
The hypothesis is rejected if an Al-substituted alloy reduces density by less than 5% or loses more than 15% of yield strength at either test temperature.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline HfMoTaTiZr contains no Nb, yet the intervention repeatedly describes a minor adjustment or increase in Nb rather than explicitly introducing Nb as an additional alloying element. The resulting composition is therefore undefined.

The intervention specifies replacing about 20 at.% of Hf, which can mean 20% of the Hf inventory, whereas the experiment specifies 10, 20, and 30 at.% Al substituting for Hf, apparently as absolute alloy fractions. These percentage bases are inconsistent; in a nominally equiatomic five-element baseline, 30 at.% Al cannot solely replace the initial Hf fraction.

The hypothesis concerns a controlled target substitution near 20%, but the rule declares the hypothesis falsified if any tested substituted composition fails, including non-target 10% or 30% variants. Failure of an off-target dose does not logically contradict the target-dose hypothesis.
